## Learning notes: Swing Trading — Trading Wiki

Holding positions across sessions, commonly for days or weeks. Review schedules and chart intervals vary; gaps and execution risks remain.

Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.

### Publisher and editorial transparency

Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date; the About page explains the site's editorial approach.

### In depth

Swing trading describes a holding-period style in which positions commonly remain open across multiple sessions. It is not a standardized contract or proof that a particular schedule suits someone with a job or school commitments. Prices can gap during closed sessions, and an intended exit can execute at a different price or fail during a halt or outage. Chart intervals and review schedules are choices rather than universal professional standards. Compare holding windows using matching dates, costs and assumptions, keeping missed reviews and adverse cases in the record.

TradeHQ’s instant practice fills omit real order-book execution.

### Key points

* Holds positions days to weeks to capture medium-term moves
* Chart intervals are choices for the stated exercise rather than a universal requirement
* Time requirements vary with the process and instruments; no universal daily schedule is established

### Why it matters when you are learning

Compare a multi-day holding window with a shorter one, including gaps between observations. No holding period is a universal best starting method for beginners.

### Worked exercise and its limits

A hypothetical share bought at $50 with an intended manual exit at $48 opens at $45 next session. For 20 shares, loss at $45 is $100 before costs, not the intended $40. Holding across sessions leaves gap and execution exposure.

## Learning notes: Day Trading — Trading Wiki

Day trading means opening and closing positions within a trading day. It reduces exposure to overnight moves while retaining intraday price, execution and cost risks; no universal loss rate is asserted.

Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.

### Publisher and editorial transparency

Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date; the About page explains the site's editorial approach.

### In depth

Day trading describes opening and closing positions within the same trading day. Fully closing a position removes that position’s later price exposure, but an intended close can be interrupted by a halt, outage or liquidity shortage. Frequent transactions can make spread, commission and slippage important even when gross gains look positive. Neither full-time screen use nor a fixed number of transactions establishes competence or profitability. Margin and account requirements depend on current venue, broker and jurisdiction rules. This entry does not assert a universal retail loss rate.

TradeHQ is a virtual spot simulator, not a brokerage or a margin account.

### Key points

* All positions opened and closed within the same trading day
* Published research and broker disclosures often report high loss rates among retail day traders; the exact rate varies by market, time period, and sample
* Real account margin and day-trading requirements depend on current rules, broker and jurisdiction

### Why it matters when you are learning

Compare the time demands and assumptions of swing and intraday examples; practice profit alone does not establish readiness for real-money trading.

### Worked exercise and its limits

A hypothetical 100-share purchase at $20 and sale at $20.10 gains $10 gross. If total modeled costs are $12, the net result is a $2 loss. Closing the position removes its later price exposure, but does not establish that repeated intraday trading is profitable.

## Learning notes: Volume Profile — Trading Wiki

A volume profile groups recorded volume into price bins over a chosen interval. Its point of control is the highest-volume bin in that sample, not a forecast of where price must return.

Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.

### Publisher and editorial transparency

Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date; the About page explains the site's editorial approach.

### In depth

A volume profile groups observed trading volume into price bins over a stated sample. The point of control is the bin with the greatest volume under those settings. A value area encloses a selected share of volume using a specified construction method; a commonly chosen 70% share is not automatically one standard deviation or an economic valuation. Bin width, observation window and data coverage affect the result. A high-volume bin describes earlier activity and need not attract future price. TradeHQ does not supply a standard historical volume-profile overlay; a separate invented table is sufficient to learn the arithmetic.

### Key points

* Plots volume horizontally at each price level, not over time
* Point of Control is the highest-volume price bin in the selected sample; it need not attract future price
* A chosen value-area share summarizes observed volume, not economic fair value

### Why it matters when you are learning

Volume Profile allocates observed trading volume to price bins; it does not identify who still holds positions. Its bins depend on the chosen data, interval and width; they do not establish a reliable price barrier.

### Worked exercise and its limits

Use a tiny invented sample: 20 units traded at $10, 50 at $11 and 30 at $12. With those price bins, $11 is the point of control. It summarizes 100 past units, not a forecast that the next price returns to $11. A volume profile is not implemented here.

## Learning notes: VWAP — Trading Wiki

VWAP is the average observed trading price weighted by volume over a stated period. Price above or below it describes the sample; the relationship alone does not establish future direction.

Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.

### Publisher and editorial transparency

Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date; the About page explains the site's editorial approach.

### In depth

Volume-weighted average price divides the sum of transaction price times quantity by total quantity over a stated sample. It weights trades rather than participants, so it does not reveal how many people are profitable or every investor’s cost basis. A benchmark comparison must specify its venue coverage and window. Some chart implementations use aggregated bars, which can differ from trade-level calculations. Price above VWAP means only that it exceeds that selected average; it need not continue or revert. Anchoring the calculation at another time changes the sample.

TradeHQ does not provide a standard exchange-volume VWAP series.

### Key points

* Average price weighted by the selected traded volume and observation window
* Price above or below VWAP describes a reference relationship, not a forecast
* A comparison benchmark whose sample and window must be stated

### Why it matters when you are learning

Recalculate the volume-weighted average for the chosen session or anchor. VWAP is a historical benchmark; price crossing it does not prove future support, resistance or profitability.

### Worked exercise and its limits

Invent trades of 10 units at $100 and 30 at $104. VWAP = ($1,000 + $3,120)/40 = $103, while the unweighted price average is $102. State the time window and trade sample. TradeHQ does not provide a standard exchange-volume VWAP series.

## Learning notes: Ichimoku Cloud — Trading Wiki

Ichimoku Cloud displays several historical-price calculations with differing lookbacks and plotting offsets. Its Kumo cloud and other lines are chart conventions, not observations of future prices.

Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.

### Publisher and editorial transparency

Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date; the About page explains the site's editorial approach.

### In depth

The Ichimoku Cloud combines five historical-price calculations with different lookbacks and plotting offsets. The linked TradingView documentation describes its components and introduces its late-1960s publication history. A line plotted ahead of the latest candle still uses historical inputs; it does not observe future support or resistance. The five components are: Tenkan-sen (Conversion Line) — the midpoint of the highest high and lowest low over the past 9 periods, serving as a fast signal line. Kijun-sen (Base Line) — the midpoint over 26 periods, serving as a medium-term trend indicator and potential support/resistance.

Senkou Span A (Leading Span A) — the average of Tenkan and Kijun lines, plotted 26 periods into the future. Senkou Span B (Leading Span B) — the midpoint of the highest high and lowest low over 52 periods, plotted 26 periods ahead. The shaded area between Senkou Span A and B forms the Cloud (Kumo) — the system's signature feature. Chikou Span (Lagging Span) — the current closing price plotted 26 periods in the past, used for confirmation. Trading signals in Ichimoku follow a hierarchy. One convention labels a bullish alignment when price is above the Cloud, Tenkan-sen is above Kijun-sen, Chikou Span is above the earlier price and Senkou Span A is above B.

The alignment describes selected historical calculations; it is not a proven strongest signal.

### Key points

* Five components that show trend, momentum, and support/resistance
* The cloud plots calculated historical values with a chosen displacement
* Component alignment describes related calculations without proving predictive strength

### Why it matters when you are learning

Identify each lookback and plotting offset. A line displayed ahead of the current candle is calculated from historical prices, rather than knowledge of future support or resistance.

### Worked exercise and its limits

On an external chart, record the lookback and plot displacement for each Ichimoku component. Moving a historical calculation forward on a chart does not make it future information. The cloud overlay is not supported by TradeHQ.

## Learning notes: Elliott Wave Theory — Trading Wiki

Elliott wave theory interprets price patterns using impulse and corrective wave counts. Different counts can fit the same observations; a chosen count does not establish a reliable forecast.

Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.

### Publisher and editorial transparency

Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date; the About page explains the site's editorial approach.

### In depth

Elliott Wave Theory is an interpretive chart framework that labels selected movements as five-wave impulses and three-wave corrections. Additional conventions about overlap and relative wave lengths are used by its proponents, but different start points and intervals can produce competing counts. Labelling a price path after seeing it is prone to hindsight bias. For an educational exercise, draw two plausible counts on one invented series, state the criteria and extend the series to invalidate one of them. Some presentations use Fibonacci ratios, but a ratio does not establish a measured chance of reversal.

No labelled wave reveals hidden orders or guarantees that a forecast will occur by a particular time. Generated simulator charts cannot validate historical predictive results.

### Key points

* The framework labels selected movements as five-wave impulses and three-wave corrections
* Wave labels depend on interpretation and can be revised
* Fibonacci levels are selected reference ratios, not established reversal probabilities

### Why it matters when you are learning

Elliott Wave provides an interpretive vocabulary. Compare alternative counts; a count does not establish trend age, exhaustion or a reliable forecast.

### Worked exercise and its limits

Ask two readers to label the same fixed historical segment before showing later data. Record disagreements and rule changes. A count revised after the outcome cannot be treated as an advance forecast or a measured success rate.

## Learning notes: Wyckoff Method — Trading Wiki

The Wyckoff method interprets price and volume through phases such as accumulation, markup, distribution and markdown. Those labels describe a framework rather than verified institutional intentions.

Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.

Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date; the About page explains the site's editorial approach.

### In depth

Wyckoff's historical framework describes selected price and volume changes with labels such as accumulation, markup, distribution and markdown. Some educators label a temporary break below a chosen range a spring. These labels are an interpretation of visible data, not records proving institutional intentions. For a hypothetical exercise, mark the range and spring criteria before looking at later candles, then compare a reversal with a continuation lower. A chart cannot identify beneficial owners, hidden orders or a verified cause for a future rally.

A chosen phase does not establish a reliable entry probability. Generated practice charts are not evidence of large traders' actual positions.

### Key points

* Four phases: Accumulation, Markup, Distribution, Markdown
* A Spring is a framework label, not an established highest-probability entry
* Price and volume interpretation does not reveal institutional positions

### Why it matters when you are learning

Wyckoff supplies a vocabulary for price and volume interpretation, without proving institutional intent. Compare alternative phase labels and record examples that do not follow the proposed sequence.

### Worked exercise and its limits

Label a hypothetical trading range using explicit price and volume criteria. Separately list evidence that would be needed to identify an actual participant's holdings. Phase labels alone cannot establish accumulation by an institution.

## Learning notes: Market Maker — Trading Wiki

A market maker posts bid and ask quotes under venue rules to facilitate trading. A quoted spread is not guaranteed profit, and obligations vary by market.

Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.

### Publisher and editorial transparency

Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date; the About page explains the site's editorial approach.

### In depth

A market maker quotes prices at which it is prepared to buy and sell under applicable venue rules. The ask-minus-bid difference is a quoted spread, not a guaranteed realized profit. Quotes can change; fills, inventory price changes, hedging and operating costs affect results. Obligations and permitted conduct differ between markets. A decentralized automated market maker is a different mechanism that applies a pool pricing rule rather than the same dealer quoting arrangement. Do not infer that a displayed quote will fill an arbitrary quantity or that a market maker always earns money.

TradeHQ does not reproduce order queues or dealer inventory.

### Key points

* Quote bid and ask prices under venue rules; liquidity is not guaranteed for every order
* A quoted spread is not guaranteed net profit
* AMMs on decentralized exchanges use algorithms instead of human market makers

### Why it matters when you are learning

Compare quoted bid and ask prices with actual executions. Spread changes can have multiple explanations and do not establish a participant’s intent or sophistication.

### Worked exercise and its limits

Hypothetical quotes: buy at $10 and sell at $10.02. Buying 100 units then selling them all at that ask earns $2 gross only if both executions occur. Inventory loss, hedging and costs can exceed that spread; a quote is not guaranteed profit.

## Learning notes: Dark Pool — Trading Wiki

A non-displayed trading venue where orders generally do not appear in public pre-trade quotes. Not every off-exchange trade is a dark-pool trade.

Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.

### Publisher and editorial transparency

Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date; the About page explains the site's editorial approach.

### In depth

A dark pool is a trading venue whose resting orders generally are not displayed in public pre-trade quotes. It differs from other off-exchange mechanisms such as broker internalisation, which may follow other rules. Non-displayed trading can reduce immediate information exposure, but fills still depend on liquidity, venue procedures and price conditions. Reporting rules vary by jurisdiction and instrument. A transaction marked 'off exchange' does not by itself prove it took place in a dark pool. For a study exercise, specify the reporting authority, market and period before comparing venue statistics.

A large reported transaction confirms an execution, not which participant was optimistic or what price will do next. TradeHQ does not model the operation of private trading venues.

### Key points

* Non-displayed venues differ from public exchanges; access and trade sizes depend on venue rules
* Current venue shares require a dated market-data source; no percentage is asserted here
* May change execution exposure but does not eliminate market impact

### Why it matters when you are learning

A reported off-exchange trade does not establish why a price moved or what the participants intended. Identify the venue, timestamp and reporting context before drawing conclusions.

### Worked exercise and its limits

Separate pre-trade visibility from post-trade reporting. An undisplayed order is not proof that the executed trade will never be reported. Check venue rules rather than infer an institution's intention from an off-exchange print.

## Learning notes: Slippage — Trading Wiki

Slippage is the difference between a stated reference price and an actual execution price. It can be favorable or adverse; volatile conditions, limited liquidity and delays may increase it.

Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.

### Publisher and editorial transparency

Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date; the About page explains the site's editorial approach.

### In depth

Slippage compares an actual execution price with a defined expected or reference price. The comparison requires a side, quantity and timestamp. Paying more than the reference on a purchase is adverse; paying less is favorable. A changing quote, limited available quantity or a delay can contribute to a difference, but a price series alone cannot isolate the cause. A limit price constrains eligible fills and may leave the order unfilled. It does not guarantee both execution and a particular outcome. TradeHQ fills supported market orders at a displayed practice input and does not model actual exchange liquidity.

### Key points

* Difference between expected and actual execution price
* Quote changes, liquidity constraints and delays can affect slippage even outside volatile periods
* Limit prices constrain eligible fills but do not ensure execution; market fills can differ from a quote

### Why it matters when you are learning

Compare expected and weighted-average fill prices, with fees stated separately. A limit price can constrain execution but may leave the order unfilled; neither order type removes every risk.

### Worked exercise and its limits

For an imagined 100-unit buy, a $10.05 fill versus an expected $10 costs $5 more. A $9.98 fill saves $2. Define the reference quote and timestamp; slippage can be favorable or adverse and differs from a separately charged commission.

## Learning notes: Impermanent Loss — Trading Wiki

Impermanent loss compares the value of a liquidity-provider position with simply holding the original tokens. The difference depends on the pool design and relative prices; fees and incentives also matter.

Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.

### Publisher and editorial transparency

Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date; the About page explains the site's editorial approach.

### In depth

For a fee-free, full-range constant-product pool initially balanced by value, compare the liquidity-provider position with holding the originally deposited assets. If their relative price changes by a factor r and arbitrage rebalances the pool, the relative value difference is 2×sqrt(r)/(1+r)−1 under these assumptions. At r=2 this is about −5.72%; at r=5 it is about −25.46%. This difference is a comparison with holding, not necessarily an absolute cash loss. Fees, incentives, concentrated ranges and token behavior change outcomes. Withdrawing does not create the earlier economic difference; a later price change can narrow or widen it.

Smart-contract and custody risks are additional.

### Key points

* Value difference between LP position and simply holding the tokens
* In a simple fee-free constant-product pool, the relative value difference grows as paired-token prices diverge
* The value difference exists before withdrawal and can change with subsequent prices

### Why it matters when you are learning

Compare liquidity provision with holding the same initial assets under a stated pool model. Fees, incentives and price changes all matter, alongside contract and withdrawal risks.

### Worked exercise and its limits

For a fee-free full-range constant-product pool initially holding 1 token worth $100 and $100 cash, double the token price. Arbitrage gives about 0.7071 tokens and $141.42 cash, total $282.84 versus $300 holding: about 5.72% less. Fees, incentives and concentrated liquidity change the comparison.

A very rapid price decline, sometimes followed by a partial or full recovery. Its causes and later path require event-specific evidence.

### In depth

A flash crash describes a very rapid price decline, often with at least a partial rebound. The term is descriptive and does not establish one universal cause or a guaranteed recovery. Liquidity withdrawal, order interactions, outages and other mechanisms require event-specific evidence. A plotted candle cannot identify a responsible participant or prove an algorithm caused the move. During a disruption, an expected quote and an executable price can differ, and orders can be delayed or remain unfilled. * Very rapid price decline; the extent and timing of any recovery vary
* Liquidity withdrawal, order interactions or errors are possible explanations requiring event-specific evidence

Use separately dated records to compare the price path and available liquidity. A sharp decline need not recover, and intended stops or limits do not guarantee execution.

Sketch a rapid price decline and partial rebound. Compare a market order submitted during the decline with an unfilled limit order. Candle shape alone cannot identify a single cause, and a fast decline need not recover fully.

pages.body:
## Learning notes: Circuit Breaker — Trading Wiki

A rule-defined trading pause. US market-wide thresholds use S&P 500 declines of 7%, 13% and 20%, with time-of-day conditions; individual-security and other-market rules differ.

Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.

### Publisher and editorial transparency

Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date; the About page explains the site's editorial approach.

### In depth

Circuit breakers are rule-defined trading pauses. In the US market-wide example described by NYSE, declines from the previous S&P 500 close trigger three levels: 7%, 13% and 20%. In a regular session, a Level 1 or Level 2 event before 3:25 p.m. Eastern leads to a fifteen-minute halt; those levels at or after that time do not halt trading. Level 3 ends trading for the day. Check the current exchange rules and special-session arrangements rather than applying this example to every venue. Individual-security Limit Up-Limit Down rules are separate from a market-wide halt: price bands and pauses depend on the applicable plan.

Neither mechanism guarantees an exit price or prevents losses, and a reopening can occur at a different price. Other markets and asset types can have different controls. For a hypothetical comparison, distinguish a 7% S&P 500 decline early in a regular session from the same decline after 3:25 p.m., then compare a Level 3 event. These are rule-reading exercises; TradeHQ does not execute exchange orders or reproduce every halt and reopening condition.

### Key points

* US market-wide halts at S&P 500 declines of 7%, 13%, and 20%
* Individual stock halts (LULD) prevent trades outside price bands
* Venue-specific crypto trading controls vary; do not assume US equity halt rules apply

### Why it matters when you are learning

Read the current venue rules and distinguish a market-wide halt from an individual-security pause. A halt does not prevent every loss or establish a post-reopening opportunity.

### Worked exercise and its limits

With a hypothetical prior S&P 500 close of 5,000, declines of 7%, 13% and 20% correspond to 4,650, 4,350 and 4,000. Apply the official time-of-day rules before predicting a halt; individual-security pauses use different rules.

## Learning notes: Pump and Dump — Trading Wiki

A fraud scheme in which promoters use false or misleading claims to inflate an asset's price and sell their holdings at inflated prices, exposing later buyers to losses.

Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.

### Publisher and editorial transparency

Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date; the About page explains the site's editorial approach.

### In depth

Pump-and-dump schemes use false or misleading promotion to stimulate buying and inflate a price while promoters seek to sell their own holdings. The SEC's linked explanation describes this mechanism for stocks; the CFTC also warns about virtual-currency pump-and-dump schemes. A scheme does not require a predictable five-stage timeline or a sale at the exact price peak. Promotion and selling can overlap, and a price chart alone cannot establish who sold or whether a statement was fraudulent. Thin liquidity can make exits difficult, but an abrupt rise or fall is not itself proof of manipulation.

Check the original claim, its date, the promoter's disclosed interests and the relevant issuer or project disclosures. A coordinated countdown, unsupported promise or undisclosed incentive warrants investigation rather than a guaranteed detection rule. Keep the evidence for a misleading statement separate from a hypothetical price scenario. This lesson explains a fraud mechanism; it does not determine whether a particular token, issuer or person violated a law.

### Key points

* False or misleading promotion can inflate a price while promoters seek to sell their holdings
* A fixed timeline, exact peak sale or price move alone does not establish the scheme
* Check claims, disclosures and promoter incentives against primary evidence

### Why it matters when you are learning

Check claims against primary disclosures and consider incentives behind a promotion. A social-media mention alone does not prove fraud, while coordinated misleading promotion warrants caution.

### Worked exercise and its limits

For a fictional promotion, list the promoter's disclosed interest, independently verifiable evidence and promised outcome. Paid hype and a price rise are warning context, while establishing an offence requires evidence and applicable law. Do not treat a suspicious message as a price signal.

## Learning notes: Risk-Reward Ratio — Trading Wiki

The risk-reward ratio compares a trade's planned loss with its planned gain. A 1:3 ratio means a planned $1 loss for a potential $3 gain; it does not guarantee those fills or establish a universal professional minimum.

Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.

### Publisher and editorial transparency

Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date; the About page explains the site's editorial approach.

### In depth

The risk-reward ratio (R:R or RRR) is a measurement that compares the potential loss on a trade (from entry to stop loss) against the potential gain (from entry to take profit target). Expressed as a ratio like 1:2 or 1:3, it quantifies the trade's payoff structure before entry, enabling traders to make mathematically informed decisions about which trades are worth taking. A 1:2 risk-reward ratio means that for every dollar risked, two dollars of profit are targeted. A 1:3 ratio means three dollars of potential profit for each dollar of risk. A planned ratio describes selected entry and exit assumptions.

A break-even calculation requires realised payoff sizes and costs; the planned ratio alone does not determine profitability. For fixed realised payoffs before costs, a 1:1 ratio breaks even at 50% wins; profitability requires more than 50%. Planned exits do not ensure those realised payoffs. With fixed realized +2R/−1R before costs, the exact break-even rate is one third; profitability requires a higher rate. At 1:3 with fixed realised gains and losses, a win rate above 25% is required before costs; exactly 25% breaks even. Under stated fixed-payoff assumptions, expected value combines the frequency and size of gains and losses.

Costs and dependence also matter, and an estimate from one historical sample does not establish a future positive expectancy. A chosen planned payoff ratio is not a universal fund rule or evidence of positive realised expectancy. The calculation is straightforward: divide the distance to your take-profit target by the distance to your stop loss. If your stop loss is $5 below entry and your target is $15 above entry, the R:R is 1:3.

### Key points

* Compares potential loss (stop loss) to potential gain (take profit)
* With fixed realized +3R/−1R before costs, 25% wins breaks even; profitability requires more
* A planned ratio is not a universal professional minimum or evidence of positive expectancy

### Why it matters when you are learning

Calculate the planned ratio, then compare it with realised gains, losses and costs. A favorable planned ratio is not proof that the outcomes will match it.

### Worked exercise and its limits

With fixed realized wins of +$3 and losses of −$1, a 25% win rate gives 0.25×3 − 0.75×1 = zero before costs. Adding any positive cost makes that result negative. Planned stops and targets do not establish realized amounts or win probabilities.

Backtesting applies stated rules to historical data to examine hypothetical results. It can reveal problems with an idea but does not validate future performance; look-ahead, survivorship and overfitting bias matter.

Backtesting applies predefined rules to historical observations under stated execution and accounting assumptions. Its results describe that selected dataset; they are not executed returns or proof of a future advantage. Look-ahead bias uses information unavailable at the decision time, survivorship bias omits failed or unavailable instruments, and repeated parameter searches can overfit the same history. * Overfitting can make selected historical results misleading

Compare three different stock-index methodologies and learn how index-tracking ETFs provide specified exposure rather than ownership of an entire market.

### Summary

Compare three different stock-index methodologies and learn how index-tracking ETFs provide specified exposure rather than ownership of an entire market.

### Source-check scope

Source check: 2026-10-31. Limited source check: ETF ownership, fund-diversification limitations and the distinction between an index and a fund were compared with SEC Investor.gov fund guidance. Named index methodology and current holdings require dated issuer documents.

### What Is a Stock Market Index?

A stock index summarizes a selected set of securities using published rules. The S&P 500 measures a large-company segment using float-adjusted market-capitalization weighting, the Nasdaq Composite measures eligible Nasdaq-listed securities, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average is a price-weighted index of 30 companies. These have different constituents and weighting methods; consult dated index methodology documents for current details.

An index is a calculation rather than a security purchased directly. Some exchange-traded funds seek to track named indexes using a specified portfolio and method. Fees, replication choices and distributions can cause a fund's return to differ from a reported index.

When a report states that 'the market' rose, identify its index, interval, currency and dividend treatment. A price index, total-return index and tracking ETF are distinct observations.

### How ETFs Work

An ETF has shares that trade on an exchange and pursues an objective specified in its prospectus. Examples include SPY (S&P 500), QQQ (Nasdaq-100) and DIA (Dow Jones Industrial Average). An ETF shareholder owns shares of that fund rather than separately registered shares in every underlying company. Holdings, fees and returns may differ from those of its reference index.

An ETF provides the exposure specified by its objective and holdings. Diversification, concentration, leverage, annual expenses and trading costs vary by fund; low cost or broad diversification is not guaranteed. Read the current fund documents before interpreting a historical comparison.

Compare ETF examples with an individual company using the same period and position value in the simulator. Examine holdings and concentration rather than treating any fund as a universally appropriate beginner investment. Several funds can hold overlapping securities.

As a hypothetical accounting exercise, compare a 60% SPY, 20% QQQ and 20% cash allocation with another allocation that also totals 100%. These are arbitrary practice settings, not a suggested beginner portfolio. Overlapping holdings can create concentration even when several instruments are used.

## Learning notes: Market Orders vs Limit Orders: Which Should You Use and When?

Compare market and limit order mechanics, fill uncertainty and the situations each order type is designed for. TradeHQ only simulates market orders.

Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.

### Publisher and editorial transparency

Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. A limited source check dated 2026-10-31 is documented below, with its precise scope. This is not a full independent editorial or professional review; no independent professional review is claimed.

### Summary

Compare market and limit order mechanics, fill uncertainty and the situations each order type is designed for. TradeHQ only simulates market orders.

### Source-check scope

Source check: 2026-10-31. Limited source check: market, limit and stop order definitions and execution/price uncertainty were compared with the SEC Investor.gov Types of Orders page. Hypothetical BTC prices are illustrative, not a verified market quotation.

### What Is a Market Order?

A market order seeks execution at available prices rather than specifying a limit price. Execution and the final price depend on available liquidity, trading halts and other conditions. The displayed quote is not a guaranteed fill, particularly when prices move quickly.

Market orders prioritize seeking execution over a specified price limit. That trade-off can involve substantial uncertainty in the eventual fill. Compare hypothetical outcomes under different liquidity and gap assumptions rather than prescribe one order type for every urgent situation.

Slippage is the difference between an expected price and the actual fill. Its size varies with order size, liquidity and timing; it is not always pennies in a named asset. TradeHQ uses simplified practice market fills and does not reproduce every exchange execution condition.

### What Is a Limit Order?

A limit order specifies the highest acceptable price for a buy or the lowest acceptable price for a sale; an execution may occur at a better price. A buy limit order executes only at your specified price or lower; a sell limit order executes only at your specified price or higher. Unlike market orders, limit orders give you price control but don't guarantee execution.

In a hypothetical example, suppose Bitcoin is quoted at $68,000 while a buy limit is set at $65,000. If the market reaches that level, the order becomes eligible to fill, subject to available liquidity and order priority. If it never reaches $65,000, the order remains open until you cancel it or it expires.

Limit orders can be useful when price control matters more than immediate execution. They are commonly used for planned entries and exits, but the trade-off is that the order may not fill at all, or may fill only partially, if there is not enough matching liquidity.

### When to Use Each Order Type

A market order and a limit order make different trade-offs between seeking execution and controlling price. For a learning exercise, compare possible fills during a liquid session, a wide spread and a price gap. Neither urgency nor a familiar ticker guarantees a small execution cost.

A limit order specifies a maximum buy price or minimum sell price. Price control does not guarantee any fill or a full fill, even when a chart touches the level. Compare an unfilled order with a partial fill and a completed fill in a written hypothetical example.

Apple and Microsoft are both large technology companies, but their business mixes differ. Apple combines consumer hardware with services and capital returns, while Microsoft combines enterprise software, cloud infrastructure and AI-related products. * Network use and ETH price measure different things. Gas is the unit used to measure transaction work; the network fee is paid in ETH. A busy network can change fees without producing a matching percentage change in the exchange price.
* Staking helps secure Ethereum, while layer-two networks handle activity with a different fee structure. These concepts explain how the network works; a TradeHQ price chart does not measure staking rewards, network demand or the effect of a particular headline.

* Separate the virtual spot transaction fee from any Solana- or Ethereum-style on-chain network charge, which the simulator does not execute.
